supportingPages.title: Counterbalanced Reasons
supportingPages.description: The Nyaya taxonomy of inferential failure has five canonical members. Most of them name ways an offered reason fails to do its work — a reason that appears in cases where the property is absent (*anaikāntika*), a reason that actually entails the opposite (*viruddha*), a reason that has not been established (*asiddha*), a reason whose conclusion has been ruled out by a stronger means (*bādhita*). *Satpratipakṣa* is the odd one out. It does not name a reason that fails; it names a situation in which an offered reason is individually sound, but a contrary reason — equally sound — is in play for the opposite conclusion.

supportingPages.title: Non-perception as Knowledge
supportingPages.description: Walk into the kitchen and notice the pot is not on the counter. You know the pot is absent. By what cognitive route? You are not inferring its absence from premises; you are not perceiving its absence in the way you perceive the counter. The Mimamsakas argued that this is a distinct kind of cognition — *anupalabdhi*, the non-perception of what would have been perceived if present — and that it deserves its own status as a *pramāṇa*.

supportingPages.title: Postulation from Inexplicability
supportingPages.description: The canonical example: Devadatta is fat. He does not eat during the day. The two observations together are incoherent without a third fact — Devadatta must eat at night. The Mimamsakas argue that the third fact is genuinely known, by its own cognitive route. There is no perception of it; there is no general rule from which it has been inferred. What forces the knowledge claim is the requirement that the observed facts cohere.

supportingPages.title: Test of Commitments
supportingPages.description: *Tarka* is the Nyaya procedure of saying: "if this claim were not true, what would follow?" — and then watching the implications. If the implications are absurd, contradict observation, or violate a more settled commitment, the original claim is supported by the failure of its denial. If the implications are coherent, the original claim is not yet supported and needs other work.

supportingPages.title: Four Aims for Human Flourishing
supportingPages.description: The classical Indian tradition names four aims that together constitute a full human life. They are called *puruṣārtha*s — literally "the aims of the human." The four are *dharma*, *artha*, *kāma*, and *mokṣa*. The list is older than systematic philosophy; it appears in the Epics, in Dharmaśāstra, in early ritual literature, and is treated as the basic frame within which other questions about how to live are asked.
